title: Restoring the Economics of Copper Processing
gist: U.S. copper smelting has shrunk to two plants processing about a third of domestic consumption, while Chinese-driven overcapacity has pushed spot TC/RCs to zero or negative, making by-products like sulfuric acid the core of smelter profitability and squeezing non-Chinese merchant smelters in Japan, Australia and the Philippines. The report recommends targeting the $1-4 billion capex gap with an expanded 45X credit for copper, a temporary TC/RC floor with offtake for allied smelters (modeled on the MP Materials deal), and keeping refined cathode from allies tariff-free until U.S. capacity exists.

insights.claim: In 2024 the U.S. consumed 1.6 million tonnes of copper, mined 1.2 million tonnes, but smelted only 585,000 tonnes — about a third of consumption — with USGS putting net import reliance for refined copper at 45 percent.
insights.so_what: The U.S. copper bottleneck is midstream processing, not mining, so domestic mine expansions alone won't reduce cathode import dependence.
insights.quote: The discrepancy is not at the mine; it is in the middle of the supply chain.

insights.claim: The U.S., a net refined-copper exporter as recently as 1976 with 16 primary smelters, now has just two: Rio Tinto's Kennecott in Utah and Freeport-McMoRan's Miami plant in Arizona, so much U.S. concentrate is shipped abroad and bought back as cathode.
insights.so_what: Existing U.S. smelters are strategic, scarce assets; new U.S. smelter projects are a policy priority.

insights.so_what: AI buildout is a major incremental source of U.S. copper cathode demand, worsening the processing gap.

themes.theme: TC/RC collapse and the new smelter economics

insights.claim: Spot treatment and refining charges have collapsed to zero or negative because Chinese-led smelting capacity has grown faster than mine supply for over a decade, with merchant smelters in some cases paying miners to secure concentrate.
insights.so_what: Bargaining power and margin have shifted to miners; merchant smelters face sustained margin compression.
insights.quote: merchant smelters are effectively competing for feedstock and in some cases even paying miners to secure supply

insights.claim: Mine supply is constrained by declining ore grades, limited new project development, and diversion of material into leaching-based production (heap leach SX-EW), common in the U.S., Chile and DRC.
insights.so_what: Structural concentrate tightness supports miner economics and keeps TC/RCs depressed.

insights.claim: Vertically integrated producers in the U.S. and Latin America capture value across mining and processing and are naturally hedged against processing margin swings, while merchant smelters in China, Japan and South Korea depend directly on TC/RC pricing.
insights.so_what: Integrated miner-smelters are structurally advantaged versus stand-alone Asian merchant smelters in this cycle.

insights.claim: With TC/RCs at or below zero, processing fees no longer cover operating costs in many regions, so smelter profitability now depends primarily on by-products such as sulfuric acid and precious metals.
insights.so_what: Smelter valuations should be driven by by-product markets (acid, gold, silver, tellurium) rather than processing fees.

insights.claim: TC/RCs are a key indicator of processing market conditions: rising charges signal ample concentrate and smelter bargaining power, falling charges signal tight concentrate supply.
insights.so_what: Track annual TC/RC benchmarks as a leading indicator of copper concentrate tightness.

themes.theme: Cost structure and China's competitive advantage

insights.claim: Smelting direct cash costs are about 20 cents per pound (around $450/tonne), with energy 30-40 percent of operating costs; global average smelter cash costs are expected to rise 5 percent year-on-year in 2026 on Middle East-driven energy price increases.
insights.so_what: Rising energy costs further squeeze already negative-margin merchant smelters.
insights.locator: Cost Structure and Industry PressureAlthough mining
insights.speaker: CSIS

insights.claim: Smelting operating costs range from about 10 to 70 cents per pound: China sits at the low end, Europe at the high end due to energy and regulatory costs, and Chile faces high costs despite being the largest copper producer.
insights.so_what: European and Chilean smelters are most at risk of closure absent support.
insights.locator: On a pure operating cost basis
insights.speaker: CSIS

insights.claim: China's smelting advantage stems from scale (over half of global refined copper production), low labor and policy-supported electricity costs, modern high-utilization plants, and a large domestic sulfuric acid market from fertilizer, chemical and mining demand.
insights.so_what: China's cost lead is structural, not cyclical, implying persistent pressure on allied smelters.
insights.quote: China’s operating cost advantage is not simply the result of lower input costs.

insights.claim: Smelters produce 2.5-4.0 tonnes of sulfuric acid per tonne of refined copper; after the U.S.-Iran conflict and Strait of Hormuz closure tightened sulfur markets, sulfuric acid's share of refined nickel production costs rose from about 26 to 42 percent and of rare earths from about 5 to 22 percent.
insights.so_what: Sulfuric acid is now a strategic input; acid-producing smelters gain, while nickel and rare earth processors face sharp cost inflation.
insights.quote: For refined nickel, sulfuric acid accounted for approximately 26 percent of production costs before the war in Iran, rising to 42 percent afterward.

themes.theme: Capex gap and the 45X tax credit fix

insights.claim: Recent Chinese smelter projects (Jinchuan's Fangchenggang expansion and Jinchang smelter, and Yangxin Hongsheng Copper) cost roughly $2,000-3,100 per annual tonne of capacity, versus about $5,700/tonne for Freeport's $3.7 billion Manyar smelter in Indonesia.
insights.so_what: Western smelters face roughly double China's capital intensity, a key competitive handicap.

insights.claim: Falcon Copper plans a roughly $2 billion, 400,000-tonne-per-year greenfield smelter in Arizona, a U.S.-Japan investment framework priority project; Fastmarkets estimates $1.8-2.5 billion for a modern smelter, but early estimates tend to rise as seen at Manyar.
insights.so_what: Expect cost overruns on announced U.S. smelter projects; Falcon Copper is a project to watch.

insights.claim: Using a conservative $5 billion benchmark, a U.S. greenfield smelter of 300,000-600,000 tonnes faces an incremental capital disadvantage of roughly $1-4 billion versus a comparable Chinese plant, and federal support should cover only that gap.
insights.so_what: Sizes the likely scale of federal support for U.S. smelter projects.

insights.claim: Congress in 2025 voted to phase out the IRA Section 45X credit for critical minerals beginning in 2031, which could expire before a new copper smelter reaches nameplate output; copper must be added to the 45X list and the phaseout repealed or extended.
insights.so_what: Legislative change to 45X is a key catalyst for U.S. copper processing investment.
insights.quote: a 2031 sunset means the credit could expire before the plant reaches nameplate production
insights.locator: Federal policy should target that gap.
insights.speaker: CSIS

insights.claim: Raising the 45X credit for copper and other critical minerals to 20 percent for the first five years, stepping down to 10 percent, would bridge the weak early-cash-flow years and crowd in private capital.
insights.so_what: A front-loaded credit would materially improve smelter project IRRs.

themes.theme: Allied price floor and tariff sequencing

insights.claim: The U.S. should offer a temporary, conditional minimum TC/RC guarantee for strategically important allied smelters tied to U.S.-backed offtake, paying out only when charges fall below a threshold and sunsetting once markets recover — modeled on the July 2025 DoD-MP Materials price floor and offtake deal.
insights.so_what: A TC/RC floor would de-risk allied smelters in Australia, Japan, Korea and Canada and extend the MP Materials template to copper.
insights.quote: A more economically coherent mechanism would guarantee a minimum TC/RCs for eligible allied smelters.

insights.claim: When a 50 percent tariff on all copper imports looked likely in mid-2025, the COMEX-LME spread surged past 28 percent (over $1/lb, about $2,600-2,900/tonne) and then collapsed after the July 30, 2025 proclamation exempted refined cathode.
insights.so_what: U.S. copper tariff headlines drive large COMEX-LME arbitrage swings — a tradable signal.

insights.so_what: A pending copper tariff determination remains a live risk for COMEX premiums and U.S. copper consumers.

insights.claim: A near-term cathode tariff would not help capacity-constrained U.S. smelters and would fall mainly on downstream users like wire and cable makers, electrical equipment, and defense suppliers; protection should follow, not precede, new capacity and distinguish trusted suppliers from strategic competitors.
insights.so_what: Copper tariffs would be a cost shock to U.S. manufacturers without boosting supply.
insights.quote: Build domestic capacity first, reconsider import protection second.
